text:
Mike R: Hey team — ran a long nsys capture for the 8k-seq generation job and the .qdrep is huge (20GB). Need quick guidance on a minimal repro + what slices to keep before I upload. I can trim to a 1-min window but worried I'll lose the latency spike.
Asha P: For long runs you usually want to 1) restrict to the hot loop using NVTX ranges, 2) capture only CUDA + NVTX, and 3) set sampling mode rather than full trace if you just need timelines. Example nsys flags we use: 
```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=cpu --output=out_short 
# or for detailed single-iteration: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --stop-on-exit --output=out_iter
```
Put NVTX around the token loop so you can zero in on the burst.
perf-bot: perf-check — baseline run exists (s3://redwood-profiling/baselines/2026-01-12/8k-gen.qdrep). If you upload a small window I can auto-compare kernel times.
Lena C: If you're going to use torch.profiler as well, enable record_shapes and with_stack so the Python side shows up: 
```python
with torch.profiler.profile(activities=[torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CPU, torch.profiler.ProfilerActivity.CUDA],
                                record_shapes=True, with_stack=True) as prof:
    model(batch)
prof.export_chrome_trace("torch_trace.json")
```
That chrome trace is useful to correlate with nsys timeline.
Kevin: Two practical tips: 1) capture a 10s window that includes the regression (not just the highest throughput region). 2) If disk space is an issue, convert .qdrep -> chrome trace and gzip: `nsys export --format=trace --output trace.json out.qdrep && gzip trace.json` before upload.
Mike R: Good — I can NVTX the generation loop. Quick Q: what's the preferred upload path? I don't want to fill the bucket with raw qdreps.
Asha P: We keep raw qdreps only for triage. Preferred flow: upload gzipped chrome trace + a tiny repro script + a link to the full .qdrep if needed. Upload to s3://redwood-profiling/eng-runtime/1772005432/ and paste link here.
Lena C: Also include the model sha + config (seq_len, batch, kv-cache strategy). If you can add a small perf log: `python tools/bench.py --model X --seq 8192 --batch 1 --iters 20 > bench.log` that helps perf-bot baseline comparisons.
Kevin: If you want a flamegraph of CPU stacks from the torch profiler, run `py-spy` or convert chrome trace to stackcollapse format and use `flamegraph.pl`. Example quick pipeline we used: 
```
nsys export --format=trace --output trace.json out.qdrep
# then use speedscope / flamegraph tools to inspect or convert
python tools/trace_to_flame.py trace.json > stacks.folded
./flamegraph.pl stacks.folded > flame.svg
```
(we have trace_to_flame.py in repo tools/)
Mike R: I'll NVTX-wrap, capture a 12s window that includes the latency spike, export chrome trace, gzip it, and upload the trace + bench.log + a tiny repro. Uploading to s3://redwood-profiling/eng-runtime/1772005432/ in ~15m.
perf-bot: perf-compare queued — once files appear I will compare kernel times and post a short report.
Asha P: If the qdrep is small enough and you want us to look at memory counters, keep the original qdrep for now and we'll stage it under `raw/` with lifecycle rule. Otherwise gzip traces are perfect.
Mike R: Uploaded: s3://redwood-profiling/eng-runtime/1772005432/trace.json.gz, bench.log, repro.zip — perf-bot, feel free to run the compare. Thank you! :pray:
perf-bot: perf-compare completed. Short summary: CUDA kernel X increased 18% wall time at the regression point, small PyTorch callstack blamelist points to attention_mask prep. See full report: https://artifacts.redwood.com/profiler/reports/1772005432/report.html
Lena C: I'll take the attention_mask prep path and try a micro-optim (vectorize a loop). If I need the full qdrep I'll request here. Thanks everyone. :thumbsup:
